summary.text: A Bernoulli trial is a random experiment with exactly two possible outcomes, called success and failure.
It is named after Jacob Bernoulli, a 17th-century Swiss mathematician who analysed such trials in his Ars Conjectandi (1713).
Bernoulli trials can also lead to negative binomial distributions, which count successes in repeated trials until a set number of failures appears.

facts.label: Die example
facts.value: Rolling a six counts as success; anything else is failure

facts.label: Coding convention
facts.value: 1 stands for success and 0 for failure

items.prompt: A die has six faces. How can rolling it still count as a Bernoulli trial?

options.label: By counting a six as success and the other five faces as failure
By ignoring any roll that is not a six or a one
By giving each face its own success probability
It cannot, because a die has more than two outcomes

items.explain: Grouping the outcomes into one event (a six) and its complement (not a six) leaves exactly two possibilities.

items.prompt: Which of these is a Bernoulli trial?

options.label: Measuring the height of one randomly chosen voter
Asking one random voter whether they will vote yes in a referendum
Recording the temperature on one randomly chosen day
Weighing one randomly chosen package of ham

items.explain: Asking a randomly chosen voter whether they will vote yes has just two outcomes, yes or no. The others give a range of measured values.

items.prompt: You roll one fair die and count a six as success. What is the probability of failure on that roll?
items.explain: The chance of a six is p = 1/6, so the chance of anything else is q = 1 − p = 5/6.

items.prompt: A statistician records every trial as a 1 or a 0. By the usual convention, what does a 1 stand for?

options.label: Failure
The first trial in the series
A trial that did not happen
Success

items.explain: Random variables describing Bernoulli trials are usually coded 1 for success and 0 for failure.

items.prompt: A researcher runs several two-outcome trials, but each one has its own chance of success. What are these sometimes called?

options.label: Poisson trials
Fair coin trials
Complement trials
Convention trials

items.explain: When multiple Bernoulli trials are performed, each with its own probability of success, they are sometimes referred to as Poisson trials.

items.prompt: Mathematicians study a whole run of coin tosses with advanced tools. What is the formal theory of such repeated trials called?

options.label: A binomial coefficient
A Bernoulli process
A single success
A die roll

items.explain: The mathematical formalization and advanced formulation of the Bernoulli trial is known as the Bernoulli process.

paragraphs.heading: Two outcomes only
paragraphs.text: A Bernoulli trial, sometimes called a binomial trial, is a random experiment that can end in exactly two ways. The two results are labelled "success" and "failure".

paragraphs.heading: Where the name comes from
paragraphs.text: The idea is named after Jacob Bernoulli, a Swiss mathematician who lived in the 17th century. He analysed these two-outcome experiments in his Ars Conjectandi, which appeared in 1713. When the trial is given a full mathematical formalization and pushed further, the result is known as the Bernoulli process.

paragraphs.heading: Everyday examples
paragraphs.text: Tossing a fair coin is the cleanest case: there are exactly two outcomes, and the chance of success is 0.5 by definition. A die can be turned into a Bernoulli trial too, by calling a six a success and anything else a failure. The die still has six possible outcomes, but they are sorted into two events, "a six" and "not a six", the second covering the other five faces. A political poll works the same way when it picks one voter at random and asks whether that person will vote "yes" in a coming referendum.

paragraphs.heading: Writing it with numbers
paragraphs.text: A random variable that describes a Bernoulli trial is often coded with 1 standing for success and 0 for failure. Write p for the chance of success and q = 1 − p for the chance of failure. For a single die where a six counts as success, p = 1/6. That leaves q = 5/6 as the chance of not rolling a six.

paragraphs.heading: Related ideas
paragraphs.text: Repeating Bernoulli trials leads to several other distributions. One is the negative binomial distribution, which counts the successes in a series of repeated trials until a set number of failures has turned up. When several Bernoulli trials are run and each has its own success probability, they are sometimes called Poisson trials instead.

paragraphs.heading: Practice questions
paragraphs.text: Two sample questions show how these trials get used. Toss a fair coin four times: how likely is it that exactly two of the tosses land heads? Or roll three independent fair six-sided dice: what is the chance that exactly two of them show a six? In the dice question, each die is its own trial, with p = 1/6 for a six and q = 5/6 for anything else.
